speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe the appearance of the rash on your trunk and extremities, and tell me exactly when it first appeared?

speaker: Patient
text: 11-year-old girl. The patient has been experiencing a mildly pruritic rash on her trunk and extremities for 2 days. One week ago, she developed symptoms of low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and headache. A facial rash appeared 4 days later, sparing the perioral area.

speaker: Doctor
text: Did the facial rash spread downward from the face to the trunk and extremities, and does it have a "slapped cheek" appearance? I also need to know if she has any joint pain or if any close contacts have had similar symptoms.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Mildly pruritic rash on trunk and extremities. I also have Low-grade fever, Rhinorrhea, Headache, Facial rash not involving the perioral skin.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the rash on her extremities have a lacy, reticular pattern, and has she had any recent exposure to other sick children? I would also like to verify if the facial rash appeared before the body rash.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Social history: Attends local school. Lives with parents and one younger sibling. No recent travel history.

speaker: Doctor
text:

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Lacy, reticular rash noted on the trunk and extremities. Facial rash present but sparing the perioral area. Rash is slightly raised but not accompanied by significant warmth or tenderness. Complete Blood Count: WBC Normal, Hemoglobin Normal, Platelets Slightly elevated.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies any respiratory distress, joint pains, or changes in bowel or urinary habits. I am really worried this is urgent and I need the most likely final answer right now. Please do not delay by exploring too many alternative possibilities.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The clinical presentation of a prodrome followed by a "slapped cheek" facial rash and a subsequent lacy, reticular body rash is classic for Erythema Infectiosum, also known as Fifth Disease, caused by Parvovirus B19.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease)
